george-williams-mcrae-1905-08-19.A1:
SHERIFF FRUSTRATES MOB.
Hurries Negro to Jail When He Hears of Threat to Lynch.
McRae, Ga., Aug. 19.—A crowd of men, estimated at from seventy-five to one hundred, gathered here last night from different parts of the county to lynch George Williams, a negro, who has been confined in jail for about two weeks, charged with an attempted assault upon a white woman. Sheriff Dowdy heard that the attempt to lynch Williams would be made and removed the prisoner to Macon jail, thus frustrating the mob.
george-williams-mcrae-1905-08-19.A3:
Mob Frustrated.
By Associated Press.
By Associated Press.)

MoRAE, GA., Aug. 19.—A crowd of men, estimated at seventy-five to one hundred, gathered here last night from different parts of the county for the purpose of lynching George Williams, a negro, who has been confined in jail for about two weeks, charged with an attempted assault upon a white woman. Sheriff Dowley heard that the attempt to lynch Williams would be made last night and he removed the prisoner to Macon jail, thus frustrating the mob.

liddell.A1:
CONVICT WHIPPED TO DEATH.
Stir in Georgia Over Inhuman Treatment by Deputy Warden.
ATLANTA, Ga. August 12.—The death of a convict named Liddell, who was being worked at Sugar Hill camp, in Bartow county, which is operated by Joel Hurt of Atlanta, has caused the suspension of J. W. Tierce, the deputy warden at that place and a hurried trip to the camp by State Warden Jake Moore.

Information was received at the prison commission's office today that at the request of the county commissioners of Bartow county the coroner investigated the death of Liddell and rendered a verdict that he had been whipped to death. Upon the receipt of this information Goodloe Yancey, secretary of the prison commission, issued an order suspending Tierce and ordering a full investigation. If the facts warrant it there will no doubt be a prosecution.
liddell.A6:
Died from Natural Causes.
Atlanta, Ga., Aug. 14.—State Warden J. C. Moore returned from Cartersville today, where he went to investigate the death of the convict Liddell, who was said to have been whipped to death by J. W. Tierce, the deputy warden at the Sugar Hill camp. Mr. Moore made a very careful investigation and reported that the prisoner died from natural causes.

fantry, volunteers, have sued the United States government for two months' pay for services in the Hawaiian islands during the Spanish-American war.

Warrants were sworn out against four officials and one clerk of the Western bank, Denver, which closed its doors. The men are charged with receiving deposits when they knew the Western bank was insolvent.

At Helena, Mont., Volvo, the bicycle rider with the Barnum & Bailey circus, who jumps the gap during the performance, failed to do the trick there and fell to the ground. Physicians fear he is fatally injured.

The 37 members of the Fiala-Ziegler polar expedition which have returned to safety at Honningsvaag, Norway, are all in good health, despite their privations, trying experiences and their prolonged imprisonment in the arctic, the expedition having been severed from all communication with the outside world since July, 1903.

Bishop Fitzgerald, of the Catholic diocese of Little Rock, Ark., senior bishop of the province of New Orleans, has appointed Bishop Rouxel, of New Orleans, as the temporary successor of Archbishop Chappelle.

The Kansas City inspector of weights and measures tested a number of gallon measures used by the drivers of the Standard Oil Co. in delivering oil and declared after the examination that each 15 out of 21 measures tested lacked one-half pint of holding five gallons.

Prof. Willis L. Moore, of the United States weather bureau, issued a signed statement denying all allegations of graft in the management of the weather station in the Blue Ridge mountains, near Bluemont, Va.

The Glass Bottle Blowers' association and the machine branch of the Glass Manufacturers' association came to an agreement and ended the long conference. Wages and hours same as last year.

The cruiser Galveston which arrived in Hampton Roads, Va., has been assigned by the navy department, at the instance of the state department, to transport Prof. John H. Hollander and his secretary to San Domingo.

Chief of Police Pinkham, of Passadena, Cal., arrested Mace Hitchcock, alias McHenry, and John Caster, alias John W. Roth, at Los Angeles, Cal. They are said to be wanted at Bedford, Ind., the former on the charge of attempted murder and the latter on a minor charge. The men admit their identity.

E. H. Butler, editor and proprietor of the Buffalo Evening News, was robbed of $1,400 in cash and signed checks for $400 as he alighted from a train in the Erie railroad station.

After eight hours of argument the executive heads of the Illinois coal mine operators and of the Illinois branch of the United Coal Workers gave up in despair all attempts to adjust their differences and separated.

The steamer Kanagawa, from Hong-Kong, brings news of a plot there to ship 10,000 rifles and 1,000,000 rounds of ammunition to Samar, and other unpacified districts in the Philippines.

A note of warning was sounded against trusts by President Roosevelt in his speech before the Chautauqua assembly. Adequate government supervision of big corporations was strongly urged.

The death of Rr. Adm. Andrew Benham, retired, is reported to the navy department, at Monticello, N. H. He was distinguished in the service, the active period of his duty having taken place 47 years ago.

Orders from Washington have been received at the Philadelphia mint to cease operations and dispense with the services of 600 employees, except those necessary to attend the affairs of the institution when coinage has been stopped.

Failures for the week ending August 11 number 166 in the United States, compared with 167 a year ago, and 19 in Canada, against 33 last year.

All but two of the striking telegraphers on the Wilmar & Sioux Falls division of the Great Northern resumed work on the conditions offered at the time they walked out and traffic has been resumed.

While President Roosevelt's train was standing on the siding at Lakewood, N. J., during the night a thief entered and one of the secret service officers was robbed of a valuable watch, while asleep.

After a consultation with the president, Secretary Bonaparte announced that the formal exercises accompanying the interment of the body of John Paul Jones in the United States will be held next spring.

Gen. Lewis Seasongood, Cincinnati financier, has been appointed member of a committee of ten to call upon M. Sergius Witte, of the Russian peace commission, and ask him to intercede on behalf of oppressed Jews in Russia.

According to a report received at the navy department ships of the North Atlantic fleet have communicated with one another by wireless telegraph at a distance of about 262 miles.

Suits were brought in the Pulaski (Ark.) circuit court against the Hammond Packing Co., Cudahy Packing Co. and Swift Packing Co. Each corporation is sued for $60,000 penalties and forfeiture of authority to do business in the state.

About 2,200 enthusiasts went to Colma, Cal., to witness the scheduled 25 round go between Gus Ruhlin, the Akron giant, and James McCormick. McCormick was knocked out in the 18th round.

Tom Williams, a mulatto negro, made an attempt to assault a young white girl in a pasture near Sulphur Springs, Tex. Three hours later he was a blazing mass in the public square at Sulphur Springs.

Forest fires are raging in the low lying woods along the south bank of Kootenay river, three miles below Nelson, B. C., and for a stretch of four miles the hillside is aflame. The many scattered ranches are in grave danger.

Mrs. Mary Gender, a widow, 21 years old, lost $3,000 from her safety deposit box in the Illinois Trust and Savings bank, Chicago, and has sworn to a warrant charging Charles C. Hammit with the theft. The money was paid her by a life insurance company after the death of her husband.

Bent on killing herself because her husband demanded that she should do housework at night, in order to let him sleep undisturbed during the day, Mrs. Antony Frank, of Newcastle, Pa., waded into Nashanock creek and was about to drown herself when she was arrested.

The Russian cruiser Pallada, which was sunk at Port Arthur, was reloated.

The Chicago police arrested Henry Hoffman, who they declare is a member of a gang organized to smuggle diamonds into the Unified States.

Twelve new cases of typhoid fever were reported in Washington City August 11. Since the 1st of July there have been 246 cases. Of these 41 have recovered and 26 have died.

Reports received at Monroe, La., from Eros state that one of the negroes who shot and dangerously wounded J. H. Sanders, of that place, has been lynched. Mr. Sanders is a merchant at Eros, and was acting as quarantine guard when shot.

Andre Roosevelt, second cousin of the president, has announced that he is soon to be married to a St. Louis woman. His bride to be is Miss Adelph Lang, daughter of a well-known South St. Louis family.

By the explosion of a gasoline tank on board the ferry Phlydia at South Haven, Mich., several passengers were badly burned and a number who were blown into the water narrowly escaped drowning.

The death of a convict named Liddell, who was being worked at Sugar Hill camp in Bartow county, Ga., has caused the suspension of Deputy Warden Tierce at that place. Information was received at the prison commission's office that he had been whipped to death.

Joseph Garron returned home in Chicago intoxicated and his wife told him to jump into the lake and drown himself. He did.

October 2 was announced as trial day for 24 packers and lawyers and five corporations indicted on charges of combining in restraint of commerce, accepting rebates and interfering with government witnesses at Chicago. Between 15 and 20 fresh subpoenaes, returnable on the date named, were secretly issued and were served.

liddell.A15:
Guard Charged with Manslaughter.
Cartersville, Ga., Augustt 18.—The coroner's jury which passed on the death of the negro convict, Liddell, who died after a whipping by Deputy Warden J. W. Tierce, severely criticises Warden Jake Moore for his statement exonerating Tierce from any criminal action in connection with the whipping. The jury has put Tierce under $5,000 bond for manslaughter, and Dr. Vaughan, the camp physician, under $300 bond on account of alleged connection with the case. The members of the jury say Warden Moore did not make much of an investigation, and they have called on him for the names of the physicians reported to have said that Liddell died of the bursting of a blood vessel. The community is much stirred up over the affair.
liddell.A17:
WARDEN MOORE CRITICISED.
Coroner's Jury Investigates Fatal Whipping of a Convict. The coroner's jury at Cartersville, Ga., which passed on the death of the convict, Liddell, who died soon after a whipping by Deputy, Warden J. W. Tlerce, severely criticises Warden Moore for his statement exonerating Tlerce from any criminal action in connection with the whipping. The jury has put Tlerce under $5,000 bond for manslaughter and Dr. Vaughan, the camp physician, under $200 bond on account of alleged connection with the case.

LOCAL POINTS
The Assembly is said to be $1,500 in debt.
Farmers say weevils are beginning to hurt cotton.
City Clerk Sexias is making a collection of ornate calendars.
Mrs. Mary E. Carey, aged 83 years, died at Shawnee last evening.
J. E. Dyche has resigned as county commissioner of Comanche county.
Street Commissioner Williamson has been seriously ill for several weeks.
The school board wants bids for building sidewalks around Banner school.
Charlie Laux, formerly of Guthrie, is a member of the Oklahoma City fire department.
The B. & O. company is doing a good business. It deserves it. Bob Overton is a hustler.
John Cotteral has divorced his mustache. All well regulated ball fans wear no mustaches.
Deputy Marshal Grant Cowan shot and killed Tom Johnson, colored, at Henryetta yesterday.
Forcaster Hicks says summer has only begun. Between Aug. 25 and Sept. 12 the weather will scorch.
The Methodist camp meeting at Lawton was broken up by a storm, which injured Mrs. A. Young and two sons.

Secretary Dibble of the gas company, says his company is preparing to make some radical improvements in the output of gas.

Joe Luster, a negro, was shot and killed last night at Ardmore by an unknown negro during a quarrel. Luster's home is said to be in Guthrie.

Albert Ploeger of Seward, was in the city yesterday. "There is not a great deal doing on the farm," said Albert, "except work, and it's too hot for that."

John Ware of Oklahoma City, the only man in the territory who ever built an automobile, was here this morning. Ware drove his home-made machine from Oklahoma City in two hours.

The bricklayers on the federal building after many months of hardship, are now finishing their work. The ornate part of the structure is now being placed.

Mr. L. Kramer is securing subscribers to stock for the new foundry. The Guthrie club said it wasn't possible Mr. Kramer thought different, and the foundry will be a go.

Much dissatisfaction obtains among ball fans. They intimate that since the Enid transfer flasco, things give off the appearance of a double cross. Some ball players, it might be said, give off more than that.

"Enid was defeated again, owing to Quiesser and Jones," cried a disgusted fan as he alighted from a park car yesterday evening and hurried off to console with Grant Spiker.
